title: Monoclonal antibodies
description: Antibody medicines and tests aimed at one exact target, now used against cancers, arthritis and many other diseases. A white blood cell that makes one chosen antibody is fused with a cancer cell, giving a hybrid that divides forever; all its descendants pour out identical Y-shaped antibodies whose tips lock onto one molecule and nothing else.
draw: A Y-shaped antibody drawn as a folded protein, the tips of both arms gripping matching knobs on the surface of a cell like keys in locks; several more identical Y shapes drift nearby, all the same size and shape.
flag: 1975 is Köhler and Milstein's hybrid-cell method (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge; Nobel 1984), the date history books give. First diagnostic kits about 1981; first approved antibody drug 1986 (OKT3, against kidney-transplant rejection). Köhler was German, Milstein Argentine-born.

title: Home blood-glucose meter
description: Lets people with diabetes check their own blood sugar several times a day and adjust their insulin. A pricked finger puts a drop of blood on a strip whose pad holds an enzyme that reacts with sugar and darkens a dye; the meter shines a light on the pad and reads how much comes back, darker meaning more sugar.
draw: A hand-held meter with a small digital screen, a test strip pushed into its slot; a fingertip with a bead of blood touches the pad at the strip's free end, and a light inside the meter shines on the underside of the coloured pad.
flag: Ames's Glucometer (Elkhart, Indiana) went on sale for home use in November 1981; Ames's Dextrometer (1980) and Boehringer Mannheim's Accu-Chek (Germany) were near-simultaneous. Ames's Reflectance Meter (Anton Clemens, 1970) was for doctors' offices. Today's meters measure a tiny electric current instead of a colour. Overlaps Rapid test strip and Continuous glucose monitor.

title: Ivermectin
description: Kills parasitic worms, mites and lice; yearly doses have nearly wiped out river blindness in parts of Africa. Made from a substance a soil bacterium produces, it jams open a gate found only in the nerve and muscle cells of worms and insects, so charged chlorine atoms flood in and the parasite is paralysed.
draw: A village health worker holding out two small white tablets on an open palm to a child who stands against a tall wooden measuring pole painted in coloured bands, the band level with the child's head deciding the dose.
flag: 1981 is the veterinary launch; approved for people against river blindness in 1987, when Merck began giving it away free. Ōmura (Kitasato Institute) found the bacterium in soil near a golf course in Japan in 1974; Campbell's Merck team found its worm-killing power. Nobel 2015 for both.

title: Geographic information system
description: Lets planners, utilities, farmers and armies ask questions of maps by computer, such as which homes lie on flood-prone ground near a river. Each kind of information, from roads and soils to pipes and land use, is stored as its own layer pinned to the same map coordinates, so the computer can overlay them and pick out where conditions coincide.
draw: A stack of transparent map sheets floating one above another, perfectly aligned over the same patch of land: the bottom one coloured by soil type, then one with a winding river, then one with roads, then one with house outlines; a few houses on the top layer glow where they sit above the river's flood zone.
flag: Changed from 1982: Tomlinson's Canada Geographic Information System, built 1963-68 for the Canada Land Inventory, was the first working GIS (IEEE Milestone 'First GIS, 1962-1968'). 1982 is Esri's ARC/INFO, the first widely sold GIS package; restore it if the card means GIS as a commercial product.

title: Computer-aided design
description: Lets engineers and architects draw on a computer instead of a drawing board. Each line, arc and surface is stored as exact numbers, the coordinates of its ends and the curve between them, rather than as ink, so a drawing can be zoomed, measured, changed and copied without redrawing, and sent straight to machines that cut the parts.
draw: An office desk with a 1980s personal computer: the screen shows a machine part as a clean line drawing in white on black, with thin dimension lines and arrows but no readable numbers; a hand on a mouse beside the keyboard, a crosshair cursor on the screen snapping to a corner of the part.
flag: Kept 1982 (AutoCAD on personal computers), matching the PC-and-mouse hint, but computer drafting is older: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (MIT, 1963), GM's DAC-1 (1964), and CAD systems sold to industry through the 1970s (Computervision; Dassault's CATIA, 1977). A case for an earlier year if the card means CAD in general.

title: Computer-generated imagery
description: Puts on screen things that were never in front of a camera, from film monsters to whole animated films. Every object is built as a mesh of tiny flat triangles; for each dot of the picture the computer works out how light from the lamps bounces off those surfaces into the camera, giving colour, shine and shadow, 24 pictures for every second of film.
draw: A teapot sitting on a chequered floor under a single lamp, its left half drawn as a bare wire mesh of small triangles and its right half smoothly rendered, glossy, with a bright highlight on its belly and a soft shadow falling on the floor away from the lamp.
flag: Collective. 1982 is Tron (MAGI, Triple-I and others) and Star Trek II's Genesis sequence (Lucasfilm), the first big feature-film uses. Earlier: flat computer images in Westworld (1973), a 3D hand and face in Futureworld (1976). First all-computer feature film: Toy Story (1995).

title: Relational database
description: Keeps the records of banks, airlines, hospitals and websites, letting thousands of people search and update them at once. Data sits in plain tables of rows and columns, linked by shared values such as a customer number; you state what you want in a short query language, and the software works out the fastest way to find and join the matching rows.
draw: Two grids of cells floating side by side like small spreadsheets with blank cells, one row in each highlighted, a glowing line joining the first cell of one highlighted row to the matching cell in the other; behind them, a tall server cabinet with stacked disk drives and blinking lights.
flag: Changed from 1983: Oracle sold the first SQL relational database in 1979 (Honeywell's MRDS, 1976, is a lesser-known earlier claim); 1983 is IBM's DB2, when they spread. Codd's founding paper was written at IBM San Jose in 1970; IBM's System R research prototype (1974-79) created SQL.

title: Local area network
inventor: Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs, Xerox PARC
description: Wires the computers in an office or home together so they can share files, printers and the internet. Each machine sends data in short packets over a shared cable, listening first; if two start at the same moment, they hear the clash, both stop, and each waits a random instant before trying again. Today a switch usually gives each its own cable.
draw: An office wall with one thick cable running along it at desk height; several desktop computers sit below, each joined to it by a thin drop cable clamped on with a small box, and a bright pulse of light travels along the thick cable from one computer toward the others.
flag: Title dropped '(Ethernet)': brackets are for acronyms, and Ethernet began as a Xerox trademark. Year changed from 1983 to 1973: Metcalfe and Boggs had it running at Xerox PARC by November 1973, linking Alto computers and laser printers (the GUI card is likewise dated by internal Xerox use). First published 1976, DEC-Intel-Xerox standard 1980, first products 1981, IEEE standard 1983.

title: Neodymium magnet
inventor: Masato Sagawa, Sumitomo Special Metals; John Croat, General Motors
description: The strongest permanent magnet, small enough for earbuds and strong enough for electric-car motors and wind turbines. An alloy of neodymium, iron and boron is ground to powder, lined up in a magnetic field, pressed and baked solid, then magnetised; its crystals hold their magnetism so stubbornly that a disc the size of a coin can lift several kilograms of steel.
draw: A shiny silver, coin-sized disc magnet held between finger and thumb, a heavy steel spanner hanging from its underside by magnetism alone, with a few iron filings bristling up from the disc's edge.
flag: Sagawa (sintered, Japan) and Croat (melt-spun, Detroit) found the alloy independently and announced it together in 1983; Sumitomo began production in 1984. The magnets are nickel-plated because the alloy rusts. Overlaps the Rare-earth magnet card (samarium-cobalt).

title: Desktop publishing
description: Lets one person with a computer lay out a newsletter, magazine or book that prints looking professionally typeset. Text and pictures are arranged on an on-screen page that matches the printed one; the page goes to a laser printer as a description of shapes, so each letter is drawn from its outline at the printer's full sharpness.
draw: A beige 1980s desktop computer with a separate square monitor showing a two-column newsletter page, its text as grey lines and one picture box; beside it a desktop laser printer feeding out the same page, the printed sheet half emerged.
flag: 1985 brought together Apple's LaserWriter printer, Adobe's PostScript page language and Aldus PageMaker; Aldus's Paul Brainerd coined the term.

title: DNA fingerprinting
description: Identifies a person, or their parents, from a speck of blood, hair or saliva. Everyone's DNA has short stretches repeated over and over, the number of repeats differing between people. The DNA is cut up and pulled through jelly by an electric current, which sorts the pieces by length into a pattern of bands unique to each person.
draw: A gloved hand pointing at a sheet of film laid on a glowing light box; the film shows several vertical lanes of dark horizontal bands like barcodes, and two neighbouring lanes have their bands at exactly the same heights.
flag: Changed from 1986: first used in a real case in 1985, an immigration dispute over a Ghanaian-British boy, published that year. 1986 is the first criminal case (the Narborough murders, clearing Richard Buckland); the first conviction, of Colin Pitchfork, was 1988. Jeffreys discovered the method in September 1984.

title: Rolling suitcase
description: Lets travellers pull their luggage instead of carrying it. Two small wheels are set into the bottom corners of an upright case, and a handle slides up out of the top on telescoping tubes; tipping the case back onto its wheels puts most of its weight over the axle, so the hand only steadies it and pulls.
draw: Side view of a traveller walking away from the viewer through an airport hall, an upright suitcase trailing behind them and leaning toward them, resting only on the two small wheels at the bottom edge of its face nearest them; the long metal handle rises out of the top of that same face to their hand.
flag: Plath, a Northwest Airlines pilot, built the two-wheeled, telescoping-handle case in 1987 and sold it to aircrews, then the public (Travelpro). Bernard Sadow patented a four-wheeled suitcase pulled flat by a strap in 1970.

title: Medical abortion pill
description: Ends an early pregnancy with pills instead of surgery. A pregnancy needs the hormone progesterone to keep the lining of the womb in place; mifepristone fits into the cells' progesterone receptors without switching them on, so the lining breaks down. A second drug, misoprostol, taken a day or two later makes the womb contract and empty.
draw: A clinic table with a glass of water and a blister pack holding one pale yellow tablet, and beside it four smaller white tablets in a separate strip; a hand rests on the table next to them.
flag: Mifepristone (RU-486) was made at Roussel Uclaf in 1980 and approved in France in September 1988 (China approved it the same year). Pairing it with misoprostol became standard in the 1990s.

title: Direct-to-home satellite TV
description: Brings hundreds of TV channels to any home with a clear view of the sky. A satellite 36,000 km above the equator circles once a day, so it hangs over one spot and beams down microwaves; a small dish focuses them onto a receiver head, which amplifies the faint signal and lowers its frequency so it can run down a cable to the TV.
draw: A small satellite dish fixed to the wall of a house: an oval dish facing up toward the sky at a slant, with a short arm sticking out from its lower edge holding a small receiver head that points back at the middle of the dish, and a cable running from the head down the wall.
flag: 1989 is Sky's launch on SES's Astra 1A satellite, the first mass-market small-dish service (Europe). Japan's NHK broadcast to small dishes from 1984, and big-dish home reception was common in the rural US from about 1980. Overlaps Communications satellites.

title: Digital cellular network (2G)
description: Made mobile phones cheap enough for billions of people, with clearer calls and text messages. The phone turns speech into compressed numbers and sends them in short bursts; each radio channel is shared by eight calls taking turns, each getting one time slot in eight. A small chip card in the phone, the SIM, proves who is paying.
draw: A small 1990s mobile phone lying face down with its back cover and battery taken off, showing a thumbnail-sized card with gold contacts slotted into a holder inside; a stubby antenna on top and a keypad visible at the edge.
flag: First call on the GSM network, Finland, 1 July 1991 (Radiolinja). The standard was written by a pan-European committee (CEPT, then ETSI), so credit is collective. Overlaps Mobile phone (1983).

title: Motion-sensor chip (MEMS)
description: The accelerometer shrunk onto a silicon chip, cheap enough to fire airbags and turn phone screens. Etching carves a tiny weight hung on silicon springs, with comb-like fingers interleaved with fixed ones; when the chip speeds up or tilts, the weight lags, the gaps between the fingers change, and the chip senses the change in stored electric charge.
draw: A greatly magnified view inside a chip: a flat silicon plate suspended above the base on thin zigzag springs anchored at its corners, with rows of comb fingers sticking out of its sides that slot, without touching, between rows of fixed fingers; the plate is shifted slightly to one side, narrowing the gaps on that side.
flag: Title changed from 'MEMS motion sensors' to put a plain name first. Analog Devices announced its airbag accelerometer chip (ADXL50) in 1991, in volume production 1993. Silicon accelerometers were made in labs from 1979 (Stanford). Gyroscope chips, which sense turning with a vibrating mass, followed in the late 1990s.

title: Matrix barcode (QR code)
description: Stores a web address, ticket or payment in a square of black and white blocks that any phone camera can read. Three large corner squares tell the reader where the code is and which way up it lies, so it reads at any angle; extra error-correcting blocks let it be read even with nearly a third of it smudged or torn.
draw: A phone held over a café table, its camera screen framing a square pattern of small black and white blocks printed on a card lying at an angle on the table; the pattern has three larger nested squares, in its top-left, top-right and bottom-left corners only.
flag: Title changed: 'QR Code' is a Denso Wave trademark (freely licensed, so widely treated as generic); Boris may prefer plain 'QR code'. Made to track car parts at Toyota factories. Overlaps Barcode scanner.

title: Contactless card
description: Pays a fare or a bill with a tap, with no battery in the card. A coil of wire loops around the card's edge; the reader's coil makes a rapidly changing magnetic field that induces a current in it, powering the chip, which answers by switching its coil's load on and off, a flicker the reader detects.
draw: A see-through view of a plastic card held flat a few centimetres in front of a reader on a bus: a flat coil of wire looping several times around inside the card's edge, its two ends joined to a tiny chip, and a matching coil visible behind the reader's face.
flag: Changed from 1995: Seoul's bus card was trialled October-December 1995 and opened as a paid service in June 1996, the first contactless card in everyday use, built on Mikron's Mifare chip (Austria, 1994). Hong Kong's Octopus followed in 1997. Location is where it was first used.

title: Electronic stability control
description: Stops a car skidding out of a bend. Sensors compare where the driver is steering with how fast the car is really turning; if it starts to spin or plough straight on, a computer brakes one wheel, the outer front to stop a spin or the inner rear to tighten the turn, pulling the car back onto line.
draw: View from above of a car on a curving wet road, its tail starting to slide toward the outside of the bend; only the front wheel on the outside of the bend has its brake disc glowing, and a curved arrow shows the car's nose being pulled back toward the bend.
flag: Bosch and Mercedes-Benz, S-Class coupé, March 1995; Toyota launched a similar system later that year. Builds on Anti-lock brakes.

title: Home broadband
description: Gives homes an always-on internet connection tens of times faster than dialling up, over wires already there. A cable-TV line carries data in a few spare TV channels. A phone line, built for voice, is split into hundreds of narrow frequency bands above the pitch of speech, each carrying as much data as its noise allows, while calls go on underneath.
draw: A phone socket on a living-room wall with a small splitter plugged in, one lead going to a corded telephone and the other to a small modem box whose lights glow; a cable runs from the modem to an open laptop on a table.
flag: Title shortened from 'Home broadband (DSL and cable modem)'. Year changed from 1997 to 1995: cable internet came first (Jones Intercable, Alexandria, Virginia, October 1995; Rogers, Newmarket, Ontario, November 1995); the first commercial phone-line (ADSL) service was GTE's in California, November 1997. Collective: Rouzbeh Yassini (cable modems), Joseph Lechleider and John Cioffi (DSL).

title: Graphics processor (GPU)
description: Draws the moving pictures of video games, and now does the heavy arithmetic of artificial intelligence. A screen has millions of dots, and working out each one's colour is the same small sum done over and over, so the chip packs hundreds or thousands of simple arithmetic units side by side, each taking a share and all working at once.
draw: A graphics card lying flat, its cooler and fan lifted away to show a large square chip in the centre ringed by smaller memory chips, with gold contact fingers along its bottom edge; the big chip's lid is cut away to reveal a dense, regular grid of thousands of tiny identical blocks.
flag: 1999 is Nvidia's GeForce 256, which Nvidia marketed as 'the first GPU' because it did 3D geometry on the chip; plug-in 3D accelerator cards (3dfx Voodoo, 1996) and workstation graphics came earlier. The thousands-of-units design came about 2006, when GPUs also became programmable for general sums. Overlaps Deep learning.

title: Kinase-inhibitor cancer drugs
description: Pills that hold some cancers in check for years, first of all a leukaemia that used to be fatal. Some cancers are driven by one faulty enzyme, a kinase stuck 'on', that keeps telling cells to divide. The drug is a small molecule shaped to fit the pocket where that kinase takes in its fuel, plugging it so the signal stops.
draw: A folded protein drawn as a twisting ribbon with a deep cleft in one side, and a small drug molecule, shown as linked balls, sitting snugly in the cleft, filling it.
flag: Imatinib (Gleevec), US approval May 2001, for chronic myeloid leukaemia. Made at Ciba-Geigy (now Novartis, Basel) in the early 1990s and taken to patients by Brian Druker in Oregon.

title: Smart electricity meter
description: Measures a home's electricity and reports it to the power company by itself, so no one has to read the dial and prices can change by the hour. A chip samples the voltage and current thousands of times a second and multiplies them to get the power used; a modem sends the totals back over the power wires or by radio.
draw: A wall-mounted electricity meter with a small digital display and no spinning disc, its cover cut away to show a circuit board inside with a chip, a few thick wires from the house supply passing through a current-sensing ring, and a short antenna.
flag: Enel began fitting Italy's 30 million homes in 2001 (done by 2006), the first nationwide rollout, sending data over the power lines. Automatic meter reading was trialled from the 1970s (Theodore Paraskevakos).

title: Electronic cigarette
description: Delivers nicotine in a mist instead of smoke, with nothing burning. A battery heats a small wire coil wound around a wick soaked in liquid: propylene glycol, glycerine, flavouring and nicotine. The liquid flash-boils off the hot wick, and the vapour cools in the air being sucked through into tiny droplets that the user breathes in.
draw: Cutaway of a pen-shaped device: a battery in the lower half; above it a small clear tank of liquid; a cotton wick passing through holes in the tank wall with a coil of thin wire wound around its middle; an air hole just below the coil and a channel from the coil up to the mouthpiece, with a wisp of mist rising.
flag: Hon Lik, a Beijing pharmacist, invented it in 2003 and it went on sale in China in 2004. His first design made the mist with a vibrating ultrasonic element; the heated coil soon replaced it. Herbert Gilbert patented a smokeless cigarette in 1963 that was never sold.

title: Electric bicycle
description: A bicycle with a battery-powered motor that adds to the rider's push, making hills and long commutes easy for hundreds of millions of people. A sensor in the pedal crank measures how hard the rider presses and the motor adds a matching push; many, especially in China, are simply worked by a twist grip like a scooter's.
draw: Side view of a bicycle with a slim battery pack fixed along the frame's down tube and a wire running to a thick motor hub in the centre of the rear wheel; the chain, cranks and pedals are those of an ordinary bicycle.
flag: Changed from 2004: Yamaha's PAS (November 1993) was the first mass-produced pedal-assist bicycle. 2004 has no single event; China's e-bike boom (mostly throttle-driven, on lead-acid batteries) ran through the 2000s. Electric-bicycle patents go back to 1895 (Ogden Bolton, US).

title: Online maps and navigation
description: Shows any street on Earth, finds the way there and talks you through each turn. The world's maps and satellite photos are cut into square tiles at many zoom levels, so a phone fetches only the few it needs; satellite positioning places you on them, and distant computers plan the route using speed reports from millions of other phones to avoid traffic jams.
draw: A smartphone in a holder on a car dashboard, its screen showing a street map with one route drawn as a thick coloured line and an arrow marking the car's position at a junction; the same junction is visible through the windscreen ahead.
flag: February 2005 is Google Maps, built from the Rasmussen brothers' Where 2 Technologies in Sydney, with satellite photos from Keyhole (US). MapQuest gave web maps and driving directions from 1996; turn-by-turn phone navigation with live traffic came in 2009.

title: Machine translation
description: Translates text, signs and speech between dozens of languages in an instant, for free. The computer learns from millions of documents that exist in two languages, such as United Nations records, finding which words and phrases usually match which; given new text, it assembles the most likely translation. Since 2016 neural networks have done this a whole sentence at a time.
draw: A traveller holding a phone up in front of a street sign in a foreign script; on the phone screen the same sign appears, perfectly placed, but with different lettering in its place (all lettering indistinct and unreadable).
flag: 2006 is Google Translate's statistical system. Rule-based systems were in use earlier: SYSTRAN for the US Air Force (1970) and the European Commission (1976), and free on the web as AltaVista's Babel Fish (1997). The round-4 lists also proposed Neural machine translation (2016); this card covers both.

title: OLED display
inventor: Ching Tang and Steven Van Slyke, Kodak
description: The screen in most smartphones and many TVs, thin enough to bend, where each dot makes its own light. Every pixel is a sandwich of thin films of carbon-based molecules between two electrodes; current pushed through makes them glow red, green or blue, and a tiny transistor behind each one sets its brightness. With no backlight, black pixels are simply off.
draw: A thin screen panel bent in a gentle curve, one corner cut away to show its layers: a plastic base, a layer of tiny transistors, a thin glowing layer between two electrode films, and a clear cover on top; the front shows tiny red, green and blue dots glowing.
flag: Tang and Van Slyke made the first efficient OLED at Kodak in 1987. 2007 marks the first OLED TV (Sony, Japan) and mass production of phone screens (Samsung, South Korea); small OLED screens were sold from 1997 (Pioneer car radio) and on a Kodak camera in 2003.

title: Direct oral anticoagulants
description: Pills that prevent dangerous blood clots and strokes without the blood tests and diet rules of the older warfarin. Clotting is a chain of enzymes, each switching on the next until threads of fibrin knit a clot. These drugs fit into one enzyme near the end of the chain, thrombin or factor Xa, and block it directly, so a fixed dose works predictably.
draw: Cutaway of a leg vein with red blood cells streaming freely along it; at one spot on the wall a few sticky platelets cling, trailing only short, loose strands of fibrin that never knit into a mesh; a small white tablet in the foreground.
flag: Dabigatran (Boehringer Ingelheim) was approved in Europe in March 2008, rivaroxaban (Bayer) in September 2008. An earlier one, ximelagatran (2004), was withdrawn for liver damage.

title: Emoji
description: Little pictures typed into messages, so a smile, a heart or a thumbs-up travels with the words. Each emoji is stored as a number code, just like a letter, so any phone can send it; the receiving phone looks the code up in its own font and draws its own picture, which is why the same emoji looks slightly different on different phones.
draw: A hand holding a smartphone showing a chat of message bubbles that contain small round yellow smiling faces, a red heart and a thumbs-up, with the on-screen keyboard open below showing a grid of such little pictures; no readable text.
flag: Changed from 2010: Kurita's set for NTT Docomo's mobile internet (1999) was used by millions in Japan; J-Phone put 90 emoji on one phone in 1997. 2010 is when Unicode added them, taking them worldwide; restore 2010 if that is the event wanted.

title: Solar farm
description: Makes electricity from sunlight on the scale of a power station, now the cheapest new power in most of the world. Fields of silicon-cell panels turn light into direct current, each particle of light knocking an electron loose; inverters turn it into alternating current for the grid, and many panels sit on motorised mounts that tilt to follow the sun.
draw: Long rows of dark blue solar panels across flat desert, each row mounted on a single horizontal beam running north-south and tilted so the panels face the low morning sun in the east; at the edge, a fenced box of electrical equipment and a line of power pylons.
flag: Changed from 2010: ARCO Solar's 1-megawatt plant at Hesperia (Lugo), California, began feeding the grid in late 1982, on two-axis sun trackers. 2010 marks no single event; the 2010s price fall is what made solar farms the main new power source (the round-4 reason). Overlaps Photovoltaic cells (1954).

title: Rocket interceptor system
description: Shoots down rockets fired at towns, while ignoring those headed for empty ground. A radar tracks each rocket moments after launch and a computer predicts where it will land; only if that is a populated area does it fire an interceptor missile, steered by radio updates and then its own radar to explode beside the rocket in mid-air.
draw: A ground launcher, a box of twenty tubes tilted steeply upward, with one interceptor missile just leaving a tube on a white smoke trail; high in the sky its trail curves to meet a small incoming rocket at a bright burst.
flag: Iron Dome; first interception 7 April 2011, near Ashkelon. Older missile defence (Patriot, from the 1980s) was built against larger missiles and is far too costly per shot for cheap rockets.

title: Cancer immunotherapy
description: Lets the body's own immune system destroy cancer, sometimes for good, even after it has spread. Killer white blood cells carry brakes, switch proteins that stop them attacking the body's own tissue, and many tumours press those brakes. The drugs are antibodies that cover the brake switches, so the killer cells go back to attacking the tumour.
draw: A microscope-style view of a small round white blood cell, its surface studded with receptors, pressed against a larger, lumpy tumour cell; Y-shaped antibodies sit on the receptors of the white blood cell, blocking a knob on the tumour cell from reaching them.
flag: 2011 is ipilimumab (US approval), from Allison's work on the CTLA-4 brake. PD-1 drugs, from Tasuku Honjo's work in Japan, followed in 2014 and are now used more; Allison and Honjo shared the 2018 Nobel. Older immunotherapy: Coley's toxins (1890s), BCG for bladder cancer (1990), interleukin-2 (1992). Builds on Monoclonal antibodies.

title: Software containers
description: Packs a program with everything it needs, so it runs the same on a laptop as on a thousand servers. The operating system walls each container off, giving it its own view of files and network and a fixed share of memory and processor, while all of them share one system underneath, so they start in a second and pack many to a machine.
draw: A rack-mounted server pulled out of its cabinet with its lid off, its circuit board covered by a neat row of small identical sealed boxes like miniature shipping containers, each a different colour, all sitting on the same board and drawing on the same shared bank of memory chips.
flag: Docker, 2013 (dotCloud, San Francisco; Hykes is French). The Linux features it uses came largely from Google (cgroups, 2007), which ran its own services in containers before that; FreeBSD jails (2000) and Solaris Zones (2004) were earlier. Overlaps Cloud data centre; the metaphor echoes Container shipping.

title: Hepatitis C cure
description: Cures a liver virus carried by tens of millions with two or three months of daily pills. The virus copies its genes with its own enzyme; the drug mimics one of the building blocks that enzyme uses, so the enzyme builds it into the new copy and copying stops dead. Paired with a second drug, it clears the virus in over 95% of people.
draw: A strand of viral genetic material, a long chain of beads, being copied by an enzyme drawn as a clamp sliding along it, the new matching chain trailing out behind; the new chain ends abruptly where one differently coloured bead has just been added.
flag: Sofosbuvir, US approval December 2013; invented by Michael Sofia at Pharmasset, which Gilead bought. Earlier interferon injections cured about half of patients, with harsh side effects.

title: Smartwatch
description: A wristwatch that counts steps, tracks sleep, measures the heartbeat and shows messages from the phone. A tiny accelerometer chip feels every step and movement; on the back, green lights shine into the wrist and a light sensor picks up the faint pulsing as blood, which soaks up green light, surges through the vessels with each heartbeat.
draw: A smartwatch on a wrist, shown in cutaway: on the underside of the watch two small green lights glow into the skin beside a dark light sensor, and beneath the skin a blood vessel swells with a pulse; the watch face on top shows a small heart shape.
flag: Title shortened from 'Smartwatch and fitness tracker' (two devices; today's smartwatch does both). Collective. 2015 is the Apple Watch, which with wrist heart-rate bands (Fitbit Charge HR, 2015) made them mass-market; Fitbit's clip-on step counter was 2009 and the Pebble smartwatch 2013.

title: Short-video feed
description: An endless stream of short phone videos, picked for each viewer by a learning program. Every swipe, replay and pause is recorded; the program compares it with the behaviour of millions of others to predict which clip will hold this viewer longest, shows that one next, and keeps retraining itself on what people actually watch.
draw: A hand holding a phone upright, the thumb mid-swipe upward; one full-screen video of a dancer slides off the top of the screen as the next, of a cooking pan, slides in from the bottom.
flag: Title made singular, from 'Short-video feed apps'. 2016 is Douyin (Beijing), launched abroad as TikTok in 2017; Vine (2013) had short clips but a feed of people you followed. Overlaps Social media.

title: Facial recognition
description: Recognises a person from their face, to unlock a phone, check a passport or pick someone out of a crowd. A neural network trained on millions of photos turns each face into a list of numbers, a point in a space where pictures of the same person land close together; the system checks how close a new face is to stored ones.
draw: A person in a dim room holding a phone up in front of their face, a fine grid of faint red dots projected from the top edge of the phone and curving over their nose, cheeks and forehead to show the face's shape.
flag: Collective. 2017 is phone face unlock with a 3D infrared dot projector (Apple's iPhone X); learned face 'embeddings' came from Facebook (DeepFace, 2014) and Google (FaceNet, 2015). Face matching was used by police and casinos from the late 1990s, and Woody Bledsoe's experiments date from the 1960s.

title: AI image generation
inventor: OpenAI; LMU Munich and Stability AI
description: Makes a picture of whatever you describe in words. A neural network is trained by taking millions of captioned images, adding random speckle, and learning to remove it; to make a new picture it starts from pure speckle and cleans it away in dozens of small steps, each guided by the words, until an image appears.
draw: A row of five squares, left to right: the first is pure grey static; in the next a blurry patch of colour appears; then rough shapes; then a soft picture; the last is a crisp painting of a cat sitting on a sunny windowsill.
flag: 2022: DALL-E 2 (OpenAI, April), Midjourney (July) and the free Stable Diffusion (August, from Björn Ommer's lab at LMU Munich with Stability AI). The diffusion method dates from 2015 (Stanford) and 2020 (Berkeley). Overlaps Large language models and Deep learning.
